newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich re-election expected despite rumblings.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich re-election expected despite rumblings.

text.p: House Republicans were set to re-elect all their leaders Wednesday despite suggestions that Speaker Newt Gingrich should step aside until ethics charges against him were cleared up.

Gingrich, who swept into office two years ago as the embodiment of what was to have been a Republican revolution, is seeking re-election as speaker despite blame attached to him for highly unpopular government shutdowns, demonisation by Democrats and a continuing ethics investigation.

Although the party has retained control of the House in successive elections for the first time since the 1920s, it did so with a reduced majority and many Republicans campaigned partly on the theme of their independence from Gingrich.

In recent days some House members and conservative commentators have suggested that Gingrich step aside from the speaker's job while the ethics cloud lingers. But he has no rival for speaker and there has been no open "dump Newt" movement. Responding to suggestions he step aside, 15 top Republicans declared their unequivocal backing for Gingrich.

The Ethics Committee is investigating whether a tax-exempt foundation formerly headed by Gingrich was used illegally for political purposes and whether Gingrich had provided accurate information to the committee about a college course he taught.

Committee chairman Nancy Johnson, R-Connecticut, has said her panel will issue a report on its two-year investigation before the new Congress convenes in January. A finding of possible serious wrongdoing could erode Gingrich's support as he prepares for formal election as the nation's third highest elective official at the start of the new two-year Congress.
At the very least such a finding would guarantee an intensifed campaign by Democrats who have kept up a drumbeat of ethics complaints against Gingrich over the last two years.
Representative Peter King, a New York Republican, had proposed that the party's elder statesman, Henry Hyde of Illinois, move into the speaker's seat, but Hyde, 72, demurred.

"The fact is that Henry told me that he does not right now have an interest in running for speaker," King told Reuters Monday. "He's the only one that I feel would be a plausible alternative to Newt at this time ... but if Henry does not want to go forward I certainly am not going to push his name any more."

Rep Christopher Shays of Connecticut, another Republican who has raised questions about Gingrich's ethics problems, expects to vote "eagerly" for him on Wednesday, an aide said. But he said Shays would abstain in January if the results of the ethics inquiry were not known then, unless the report was being held up for partisan political reasons.

Rep Steve Largent of Oklahoma agreed with a television interviewer recently that it would be a good idea for Gingrich to step aside in favour of Hyde, but he has since said he regretted any problem his comment might have caused and would be supporting Gingrich.
In any case, Gingrich was expected to trim his sails in the new Congress. Instead of declaring a revolution he is talking about cooperation with a re-elected Democratic President Clinton.

With new members more independent than the last freshman class, moreover, he will no longer be able to turn the speaker's job of presiding over the House into an all-powerful post, as he and other strong speakers have done in the past.

Public attention may now shift to Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott, who has no opponent in the Senate leadership elections next month. Lott has the benefit of a Senate majority that increased by a net two seats in the Nov. elections while House Republicans lost eight seats.
